prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred single part, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. After the full exchange the case still rests on one thing: a quantitative prediction (the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, with a specific magic angle and flat bands) was confirmed seven years later by a surprising experimental result (correlated insulating and superconducting states, 2018) in a system whose control parameter, the twist angle, is a laboratory dial. Reproduction by many independent groups and across many moire platforms is what the prize criterion asks of a discovery. The chair's question about the mechanism is the one that matters most to me. A citation can and should be worded around the predicted flat bands and the observed phases, and say nothing about why the material superconducts; the committee has often rewarded a discovery whose explanation stayed open. The three-name limit also fits this case unusually well: Bistritzer and MacDonald for the prediction, Jarillo-Herrero for the experimental discovery. I do not count opening support as a substitute for this judgement, but I note that the opening ballots gave it the most first places and that the round-1 exchange did not produce a single argument that the observations themselves are doubtful.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are maturity of interpretation and credit. Eight years is short; the superconducting mechanism and several correlated phases are unsettled, and twist-angle disorder limits quantitative comparison with theory, as Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Pearce all stress. Experimental credit is also thinner than the three names suggest: Cao, Fatemi and the parallel moire heterostructure work of Dean and colleagues cannot be named, and Olsson's request to check the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature has not been fully discharged from what I have in front of me. Finally B012 is the more mature candidate with broader opening ranking (seven of eight), and a committee that weights settled interpretation more heavily than I do could reasonably choose it. The 2016 overlap and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission weaken B012 for me, but not so much that I would call it a poor choice.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B012 and would revisit B047 in a few years because the superconducting mechanism is unresolved and the experimental credit sits in one group.
responses.response: I accept that maturity is the real axis of disagreement, but I do not think the mechanism question is decisive. What the prize would honour is the flat-band prediction and the observed phases, which are secure; the mechanism is what researchers will work on next. I also do not see your attribution argument cutting only one way. The B012 trio leaves out the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction that pointed experimenters to HgTe, and Zhang is deceased, so for B012 the gap is in the prediction half of the chain, whereas for B047 the prediction (Bistritzer, MacDonald) and the decisive experiment (Jarillo-Herrero) are both covered, and what is left out is mostly the experimental first authors. Your own conflict note makes the same point about B004 that I would make about field closeness generally: I give your preference for B012 full weight, and I do not discount it.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B012 as the candidate most colleagues can defend, argues the Z2 invariant and time-reversal-protected edge states are separate from the 2016 prize, and says Kane and Mele are the clearest case of crediting decisive prediction plus first observation.
responses.response: I agree that Z2 and the helical edge states are a distinct discovery from the 2016 prize, and that removes most of my worry about overlap; I am now less inclined to treat 2016 as a bar. Where I still differ is on the claim that the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is the cleanest Nobel-style split. Kane and Mele made the foundational proposal, but the prediction that told Molenkamp's group which material to grow was by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, so the prediction-to-observation chain in the citation has a missing link. In B047 the same chain is intact with the same three names. I would also resist counting breadth of ranking as support for a configuration: seven members ranking B012 between second and fourth shows that it is acceptable to everyone, not that anyone thinks it the best prize this year. I keep it as my first alternative and I would not object to it.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and twist-angle disorder limits comparison with theory, would keep MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as the cleanest pair and treat Bistritzer as defensible but not equally decisive, and would not oppose B047 as second-best.
responses.response: Thank you for the concession that you would not oppose it. On Bistritzer, I stay with three names. The magic angle and the flat bands are results of the 2011 continuum model, and its first author did the calculation; a two-name prize would credit that prediction to MacDonald alone and would describe the history inaccurately. The Nobel record also has several cases of a theory and an experimental part sharing a prize with unequal roles among the names. On maturity, I accept that a few more years would make the interpretation firmer, but I think waiting is a cost as well: the field is already broad, and the discovery is not going to be less real in 2030.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B019 on maturity, argues the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes because magic-wavelength trapping solves a different problem, and would keep B047 for a later year.
responses.response: Your argument that the lattice clock is not a second comb prize persuades me; the magic-wavelength lattice is a different idea, and I now treat the novelty objection to B019 as weaker than I did in round 1. That is why B019 remains my second alternative. My remaining difference is scope and timing. The clock is an extraordinary measurement advance with the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, but part of its impact (the redefinition of the second) is still prospective, and its reach for what physicists can now ask is narrower than moire matter, where a single tunable parameter opened a whole class of correlated systems. I do not claim that this is a decisive point, and a prize for B019 would be one I could defend.

responses.point: Olsson supports B047 with all three names but asks the committee to check the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature before fixing citation wording.
responses.response: I agree with this request and have made it part of how I word the citation. I cannot verify the earlier moire band-structure literature (including earlier twisted-bilayer work on band-structure changes at small angles) from the material supplied, and I do not want to assert from memory that the Bistritzer-MacDonald result had no precedent. That is why my citation says prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene, a narrow and specific claim, rather than first prediction of moire effects in general. If the check showed that earlier work already identified the flat bands, I would reconsider Bistritzer's place; if it only showed related band-structure results, the specific magic-angle prediction would still stand.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B047 from B009 and wants the citation worded around the prediction and the observed phases, not any superconductivity mechanism; he also notes B019 could be a partner part in a two-part prize.
responses.response: I agree with your wording and I think it also answers the chair's question about the mechanism. On a two-part prize, I considered B047 with B019, but the three-person ceiling makes it impractical: B019 needs Katori and Ye, and B047 would then be left with one name, which would break the theory-experiment pairing that I think is the case's strength. A fair two-part configuration would have to shrink B047 to two names or drop one of the clock names, and I do not think either is justified, so I stay with a single part.

uncertainties: Whether the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature, which I cannot check from the supplied record, changes how the prediction should be credited or worded.
Whether the committee will treat the unsettled superconducting mechanism as a maturity bar; if a majority does, B012 is the better choice this year and I would support it.
Whether the omission of Cao, Fatemi and the parallel moire experiments is acceptable under a three-name limit, or distorts the credit more than I now judge.
How much weight to give B012's broader opening ranking against its attribution gap (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and the 2016 prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are in high-energy theory and cosmology and do not touch any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I repeat my disclosure that as a theorist I may favour candidates built on a decisive prediction, and I have tried to give the experimental maturity case for B012 and B019 its due weight; I have not changed this note from round 1.
